notes.meaning: Paul introduces himself as an apostle chosen by the will of God, not by any human choice. God sent him out to preach the promise of true, eternal life found only in Jesus Christ. Facing prison and the threat of death, Paul finds deep comfort in this promise of life.

Paul greets Timothy, calling him his dearly loved child in the faith. He asks God the Father and Jesus Christ the Lord to give him grace, mercy, and peace. While Paul usually wishes grace and peace to entire churches, he specially asks for mercy when writing to his fellow ministers who carry heavy burdens.

Paul gives thanks to God, whom he worships with a clear conscience just as his godly ancestors did. Even while suffering in prison, he knows he has not done wrong. He constantly remembers Timothy in his prayers both night and day.
Paul remembers the tears Timothy shed when they last had to say goodbye. He yearns to see his young friend again, knowing that a reunion would bring him great joy in the middle of his trials.

Paul is reminded of Timothy's genuine, unpretentious faith. This same true trust in God lived first in his grandmother Lois and then in his mother Eunice, who taught him God's truth from an early age. Paul is confident that this real faith now lives firmly inside Timothy as well.

Because Timothy has this true faith, Paul urges him to fan into flame the spiritual gift God gave him. This special gift and ability for ministry was given when Paul placed his hands on him in prayer. Like a fire that needs stirring to keep burning bright, Timothy must actively practice and use what God has provided.

differ.view: The gift refers specifically to the pastoral ministry, which requires constant effort because believers can grow careless or lazy under temptation.
The gift was the Holy Spirit granting special preaching power that only an apostle could impart by touch before Timothy's formal church ordination.
God often passes spiritual gifts through the laying on of hands, and believers should actively stir up the power they already have rather than passively waiting for a new blessing.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The laying on of hands was the sacrament of holy orders, which made Timothy a bishop and gave him an indelible, permanent spiritual character.

notes.meaning: God has not given his people a spirit of cowardice or slavish dread. Instead, His Spirit fills believers with divine power to face danger, genuine love toward God and people, and self-control to keep a calm and steady mind.

Because God gives courage, Timothy must never be ashamed to speak up for Jesus or stand by Paul, who is in prison for Christ. Instead, he should be ready to suffer hardship for the good news of Jesus, relying completely on God's strength to see him through.

God saved believers and invited them to live pure and holy lives. He did not do this because of any good deeds they accomplished, but entirely out of His own gracious plan. This free grace was already purposed and given in Christ Jesus before the world even began.

This eternal plan has now been openly revealed through the earthly coming of our Savior, Jesus Christ. By rising from the dead, Jesus broke the power of death and brought immortal, endless life clearly into the light through the gospel message.
Paul was appointed by God to serve this very gospel. He was given the work of a public herald to announce the news, an apostle sent out with authority, and a teacher to guide people in the truth.

Because Paul faithfully preaches this message, he is now suffering in chains, yet he feels no shame. He knows the faithful Savior in whom he has placed his trust, and he is fully persuaded that Christ is able to guard his life and eternal soul until the great judgment day.
Paul commands Timothy to hold tightly to the pattern of healthy, true teaching that he heard from him. Timothy must cling to this truth with faith and love, which flow from belonging to Christ Jesus.

The pure gospel message is a precious treasure that was entrusted to Timothy's care. He cannot protect it by his own human strength, so he must guard it through the power of the Holy Spirit who lives inside all believers.

Timothy already knows the painful fact that Christians from the province of Asia pulled away and deserted Paul when he was arrested and disgraced. Two prominent men among those who turned away were Phygelus and Hermogenes.

In contrast to those who ran away, Onesiphorus repeatedly brought relief and encouragement to Paul. He was not ashamed to be seen visiting an apostle who was locked up in chains, so Paul prays that the Lord will pour out mercy on his entire family.
When Onesiphorus traveled to Rome, he did not ignore the imprisoned apostle. Instead, he took great pains to search through the crowded city until he finally located where Paul was being held.

Paul asks that the Lord grant Onesiphorus divine mercy on the final day of judgment. He reminds Timothy that Timothy knows firsthand just how much helpful service Onesiphorus had already provided back in Ephesus.

differ.view: Some Anglicans hold that because Onesiphorus was likely dead, Paul's words show that limited, loving prayers for the departed can be allowable.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching points to this passage as biblical support for praying for the dead, since Onesiphorus had likely died and Paul asks for mercy on his behalf at the judgment.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox tradition sees Paul's blessing for Onesiphorus as a clear New Testament example of offering prayer for those who have departed this life.
